source1: Stuart Munro-Hay, Aksum: An African Civilisation of Late Antiquity, Edinburgh University Press 1991 (online text) - https://www.livingston.org/cms/lib4/NJ01000562/Centricity/Domain/602/aksum.pdf
notes: Munro-Hay: coin-issuing kings (e.g. Armah) reigned into the early 7th century and Aksum stayed capital until c.630; Britannica dates decline to the 7th-8th centuries. 599 is a period boundary, not an end.

successor: Monte Alban II (same Monte Alban polity)
source1: Charles S. Spencer and Elsa M. Redmond, 'Militarism, Resistance, and Early State Development in Oaxaca, Mexico', Social Evolution & History 2(1), 2003 - https://www.SocioStudies.org/journal/files/seh/2003_1/militarism_resistance_and_early_state_development.pdf
source2: American Museum of Natural History, Division of Anthropology, 'Archaeology of the Canada de Cuicatlan, Mexico' (Spencer and Redmond project) - https://www.amnh.org/research/anthropology/curatorial-research/meso-american-archaeology/projects/6.-canada-de-cuicatlan
notes: Ceramic phase without written records. Late MA I shows the first state organization at Monte Alban; the state 'continued to develop' into MA II, when Monte Alban was capital of a fully developed state. Phase boundary only.

source1: Charles Melville and Abbas Zaryab, 'Chobanids', Encyclopaedia Iranica 1991 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/chobanids
source2: Reuven Amitai, 'Il-Khanids i. Dynastic History', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/il-khanids-i-dynastic-history ; also Peter Jackson, 'Jalayerids', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/jalayerids
notes: Ruling house ended with Abu Sa'id's death 1335; amirs fought via puppet khans (Chobanids held Tabriz from 1338). Golden Horde's Jani Beg occupied Tabriz 1357 (inside W), so priority rule gives T2. Database 1339 reflects puppet era.

After Egypt withdrew in 1884, Britain concluded protection treaties with Somali clans 1884-86; no conquest of the interior. Reach of any Isaaq central authority and the 1300 start date are doubtful; sultans persisted under British rule.

source1: Larry V. Benson, Timothy R. Pauketat and Edward R. Cook, 'Cahokia's Boom and Bust in the Context of Climate Change', American Antiquity 74(3), 2009 - https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/E03CC9E66294A57EA1E2A76ED40D5C68
source2: Mary Beth D. Trubitt, 'Mound Building and Prestige Goods Exchange: Changing Strategies in the Cahokia Chiefdom', American Antiquity 2000 - https://core-cms.cambridgecore.org/core/journals/american-antiquity/article/mound-building-and-prestige-goods-exchange-changing-strategies-in-the-cahokia-chiefdom/452D7D0D9F8299DB3693A74B972B9776
notes: Archaeological phase; chiefdom inferred, not recorded. Trubitt: c.1200 marks changed leadership strategy, not collapse, so Cahokia continued into Moorehead. Benson et al.: drought, palisade (unrest), ~50% population loss by 1200 (Q4 Y); abandonment by 1350.

successor: Gahadavala dynasty (Kannauj by c.1090; after Ghaznavid sack of 1018)
source2: R. C. Majumdar (ed.), The History and Culture of the Indian People IV: The Age of Imperial Kanauj, Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan 1955, Foreword - https://archive.org/details/ageofimperialkan04bhar
notes: Feudatories broke away in the 10th century (Q4 Y). Mahmud of Ghazna captured and razed Kannauj in 1018, inside W; a Pratihara rump lingered to c.1036 (leads only). Gahadavalas held Kannauj by c.1090; interim control unclear.

source1: Jeffrey Fleisher and Stephanie Wynne-Jones, 'Ceramics and the Early Swahili: Deconstructing the Early Tana Tradition', African Archaeological Review 28(4), 2011 - https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10437-011-9104-6
notes: Tana Tradition is a coastal ceramic tradition (early phase c.600-900); 'Classic Tana' seems a later archaeological phase with no capital or core given. 1498 matches Portuguese arrival. Core and ending mode cannot be identified.

successor: Egypt under Muhammad Ali (Turco-Egyptian Sudan, Turkiyya)
source1: Library of Congress Federal Research Division, Sudan: A Country Study (ed. H. C. Metz, 1991), 'The Turkiyah, 1821-85' and 'The Funj' - http://countrystudies.us/sudan/11.htm
source2: Vladimir B. Lutsky, Modern History of the Arab Countries, Moscow 1969, ch. 7 - https://www.marxists.org/subject/arab-world/lutsky/ch07.htm
notes: Muhammad Ali's army invaded in 1820; the last Funj sultan surrendered Sennar without a shot in June 1821, starting Turco-Egyptian rule. Prior civil war and figurehead sultans; kingdom 'virtually disintegrated' (Q4 Y). Database 1820 is close.

successor: Ethiopian Empire (Shewan forces of Menelik II)
source1: Library of Congress Federal Research Division, Ethiopia: A Country Study (1991), 'From Tewodros II to Menelik II, 1855-89' - http://countrystudies.us/ethiopia/14.htm
source2: No second scholarly source could be opened (web tools rate-limited); Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Gumma' used only as a lead - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Gumma
notes: Leads only: Menelik II's Shewan forces conquered Gumma c.1885-86 and crushed Firisa's 1899-1902 revolt; LoC study confirms Shewan expansion over south-western Oromo before 1889. Database end 1897 looks late. Scholarly confirmation lacking.

successor: Kingdom of Bohemia under Habsburg kings (Ferdinand I, elected 1526)
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Louis II (king of Hungary and Bohemia)' - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-II-king-of-Hungary-and-Bohemia
notes: Louis II died at Mohacs 1526; the Bohemian estates elected Ferdinand I of Habsburg and the kingdom's institutions continued (dynastic change only). Q4: 1468-78 succession war with Matthias Corvinus; crown lands split until 1490.
